payload.rationale: No 2026 case-count data was supplied, so this rests on background knowledge through early 2026 plus transfer assumptions. Observed background: 2025 ended at roughly 2,200+ confirmed US measles cases (highest since 1992), and 2026 began with unusually intense transmission—a large South Carolina Upstate outbreak (~900+ cases by mid-February) plus ongoing Utah/Arizona-area transmission—putting early-2026 cumulative counts well ahead of 2025's pace. A plausible extrapolation is that 2026 surpassed 2025's total by spring. However, measles incidence in the US historically peaks in late winter/spring and fades over summer as outbreaks are controlled and school-year mixing drops; reaching >6,000 would require roughly triple 2025's record and sustained multi-state outbreaks through the fall, or an under-vaccinated community outbreak on the scale of the 2025 West Texas event recurring several times. My central expectation for the 2026 CDC total is in the ~3,000–5,000 range, with a meaningful right tail. Too high: if spring outbreaks were contained by March–April and summer was quiet (typical seasonality), the total could settle near 3,000–4,000, making 6,000 clearly out of reach; also CDC counts only confirmed cases and revisions after expiration don't count. Too low: early-2026 momentum was exceptional, elimination status was being lost, national MMR coverage continues to decline, and large connected under-vaccinated networks could have produced outbreaks I cannot observe from my vantage; by the September 2026 cutoff the actual count may already be near or above the threshold, which would make this estimate badly wrong in either direction.
limitations: No supplied evidence on 2026 cumulative CDC case counts as of the forecast cutoff
Background knowledge only extends to early 2026; later trajectory is inferred from seasonality and outbreak dynamics
Threshold relies on CDC's confirmed-case tally as of contract expiration; reporting lag and definitions add uncertainty
